(6.4)

In this way, Theorem
2
should be thought of as placing constraints on arbitrarily long sequences of discontinuities of Feynman integrals. Of course, in many cases, this constraint will be trivially satisfied, as the discontinuities with respect to
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
will both be zero. But as seen at the end of Sec.
4
, and as we will see in further examples in this section, this constraint is not always satisfied in this trivial way.

6.1
Tangential Maps

One of the requirements for Pham loci to be principal is that they correspond to singularities of type
S_{1}^{+}
. This in turn implies that the Hessian of the projection map is positive or negative definite, as discussed in Sec.
5.3
.
We now take a moment to discuss this requirement in more detail. As we will see, when
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
are principal Pham loci and
{\kappa^{\prime}}
dominates
\kappa
,
the definiteness of the Hessian leads naturally to the geometric picture that

\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
intersect
tangentially
.

In the neighborhood of
S_{1}^{+}
critical points, Morse’s lemma tells us that the projection map
\pi
can be written as quadratic form of corank one. More explicitly, if
\pi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}
with
n>p
, then one can find coordinates near the critical point such that
p-1
of the coordinates transform linearly, while the remaining
p^{\text{th}}
coordinate is a quadratic function of the other
n-p
variables in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
. To be concrete, let us say that
{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
has dimension
n
,
{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa})
has dimension
p
, and
{\mathcal{S}}(G_{0})
has dimension
q
.
We pick coordinates
x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
,
y\in\mathbb{R}^{p}
, and
z\in\mathbb{R}^{q}
, and thus have maps that can be depicted as

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\kappa^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\kappa}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\overline{\kappa}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\kappa^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces z\in\mathbb{R}^{q}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\overline{\kappa}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{\kappa}}

(6.5)

For definiteness, we take
n>p>q
; other cases can be treated similarly.
As both
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
are principal, they are singularities of type
S_{1}^{+}
and the projection maps are corank one. We now explore the forms taken by the projection maps by trial and error. For a more systematic approach, see Ref.
pham
.

Since
\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}=\pi_{\kappa}\circ\pi_{{\overline{\kappa}}}
, we begin by parameterizing
\pi_{\kappa}
and
\pi_{\overline{\kappa}}
, after which
we can deduce
\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}
.
Starting with the projection associated with
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
, by Morse’s lemma we can choose coordinates
z=\pi_{\kappa}(y)

in the neighborhood of the critical point of the form

\pi_{\kappa}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1})=(y_{1},\ldots y_{q-1}),\quad z_{q}=y_{q}^{2}+\cdots+y_{p}^{2}\,.

(6.6)

If we choose the map
\pi_{\overline{\kappa}}
to take a similar form,

\pi_{{\overline{\kappa}}}:\quad(y_{1},\ldots,y_{p-1})=(x_{1},\ldots x_{p-1}),\quad y_{p}=x_{p}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}\,,

(6.7)

then the concatenated projection is given by

\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1})=(x_{1},\ldots x_{q-1}),\quad z_{q}=x_{q}^{2}+\cdots+x_{p-1}^{2}+(x_{p}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2})^{2}.

(6.8)

The dependence of each change of coordinates thus ends up looking like:

\underbrace{\underbrace{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots x_{q-1}}_{y_{1}\ldots y_{q-1}}}_{z_{1}\ldots z_{q-1}},\underbrace{\underbrace{x_{q},\ldots,x_{p-1}}_{y_{q}\ldots y_{p-1}}\underbrace{x_{p},\ldots,x_{n}}_{y_{p}}}_{z_{q}}.

(6.9)

However, due to the quartic dependence of
z_{q}
on
x_{p}
through
x_{n}
, the singularity described by
\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}
is not
S_{1}^{+}
. Correspondingly, this is not the parametrization we are looking for.

We can instead try keeping
\pi_{\overline{\kappa}}
as it is, while we take
\pi_{\kappa}
to have the form:

\pi_{\kappa}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1})=(y_{1},\ldots y_{q-1}),\quad z_{q}=y_{q}^{2}+\cdots+y_{p-1}^{2}+y_{p}\,.

(6.10)

With these choices, we have

\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-1})=(x_{1},\ldots x_{q-1}),\quad z_{q}=x_{q}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}\,.

(6.11)

Now the singularity described by
\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
is of type
S_{1}^{+}
; however,
\pi_{\kappa}
has no critical points.

A third attempt, in which we again keep the same form of
\pi_{\overline{\kappa}}
, is to choose

\pi_{\kappa}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-2})=(y_{1},\ldots y_{q-2}),\quad z_{q-1}=y_{p},\quad z_{q}=y_{q}^{2}+\cdots+y_{p-1}^{2}\,.

(6.12)

In this case,

\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}:\quad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{q-2})=(x_{1},\ldots x_{q-2}),\quad z_{q-1}=x_{p}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}\quad z_{q}=x_{q}^{2}+\cdots+x_{p-1}^{2}.

(6.13)

Now,
\pi_{\kappa}
describes a singularity of
S_{1}^{+}
, but
\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}
has corank two. Indeed, this describes a case in which two principal Pham loci intersection transversally. We will consider this situation in Sec.
7
.

Finally, let us consider projection maps

\pi_{\kappa}
and
\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
that take the form

\displaystyle\pi_{{\overline{\kappa}}}

\displaystyle\colon\quad(y_{1},\ldots,{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{y_{p-1}}}})=(x_{1},\ldots{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x_{p-1}}}}),\quad y_{p}=x_{p}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2}\,,

(6.14)

\displaystyle\pi_{\kappa}

\displaystyle\colon\quad z_{q-1}={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{y_{p-1}}}}+y_{p},\quad z_{q}=y_{q-1}^{2}+\cdots+{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{y^{2}_{p-1}}}}\,.

(6.15)

Now both
\pi_{\kappa}
and
\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
describe
S_{1}^{+}
singularities, and we have

\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}=\pi_{\kappa}\circ\pi_{{\overline{\kappa}}}:\quad z_{q-1}={{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x_{p-1}}}}+x_{p}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n}^{2},\quad z_{q}={{x_{q-1}^{2}}}+\cdots+{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x^{2}_{p-1}}}}\,,

(6.16)

where the dependence of each change of coordinates looks like:

\underbrace{\underbrace{x_{1},\ldots x_{q-2}}_{y_{1}\ldots y_{q-2}}}_{z_{1}\ldots z_{q-2}},\underbrace{x_{q-1},\ldots,x_{p-2}}_{y_{q-1}\hskip 8.19447pt\ldots}\underbrace{{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x_{p-1}}}}}_{{{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{y_{p-1}}}}}}\underbrace{x_{p},\ldots,x_{n}}_{y_{p}}
\underbrace{\phantom{x_{q-1},\ldots,x_{p-2},x_{p-1}}}
\underbrace{\phantom{x_{p-1}x_{p},\dots,x_{n}}}
z_{q}
z_{q-1}

(6.17)

We can explicitly confirm that the projection
\pi_{\kappa}
has a singularity when all the variables that
z_{q}
depends on vanish by constructing the (reduced) Jacobian:

J_{\kappa}=\frac{\partial(z_{q},z_{q-1})}{\partial(y_{q-1}\ldots y_{p})}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}2y_{q-1}&\dotso&2{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{y_{p-1}}}}&0\\
0&0&1&1\end{array}\right)\,.

(6.18)

The determinant of this matrix vanishes, and there is correspondingly a critical point, where
y_{q-1}=\cdots=y_{p-1}=0
. The critical values of this map occur where
z_{q}=0
, for any value of
z_{q-1}
.
Similarly, the (reduced) Jacobian for
\pi_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
is

J_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}=\frac{\partial(z_{q},z_{q-1})}{\partial(x_{q-1}\dotso x_{n})}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}2x_{q-1}&\dotso&2{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x_{p-1}}}}&0&0&0\\
0&0&1&2x_{p}&\cdots&2x_{n}\end{array}\right)\,,

(6.19)

which has two critical points (both of which are
S_{1}^{+}
). The first occurs at
x_{q-1}=\dotso=x_{p-1}=0
, which gives rise to critical values when
z_{q}=0
. The second occurs where

x_{q-1}=\dotso=x_{p-2}=x_{p}=\cdots=x_{n}=0
, for any
{{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{x_{p-1}}}}
.
Its critical value is given by
z_{q}=z_{q-1}^{2}
for any
z_{q-1}
. This encodes a parabola, which is tangent to the first critical surface at
z_{q}=0
. Stated more explicitly, this tells us that Theorem
2
describes situations in which pairs of Pham loci intersect tangentially, where this intersection locally looks like the intersection of a line and a parabola.

The map in Eq. (
6.19
) describes singularities for which the tangent space of
G^{\kappa}
is smaller than that of
G^{\kappa^{\prime}}
, so
n>p
. For some contractions, such as those at one-loop, the tangent space of
G^{\kappa^{\prime}}
is more constrained by the on-shell conditions than that of
G^{\kappa}
, so
n<p
. In those cases, we need a different tangential map, which was worked out in Refs.
pham
;
pham2011singularities
. The corresponding Jacobian
J_{\kappa^{\prime}}
only has a singularity at
z_{q}=z_{q-1}^{2}
, but not at
z_{q}=0
. For example, the on-shell space of the triangle Landau diagram discussed in Sec.
4
will have a singularity at the triangle Pham locus, but not at the Pham locus corresponding to the bubble Landau diagram.

6.2
Homotopy Loops

We have now established that when we have two
S_{1}^{+}
contractions where one dominates the other, the relevant coordinates of the Pham loci near their intersection can be parametrized as line and a parabola. We now study how the homotopy group acts near one of these intersection points. Concretely, we consider a pair of Pham loci

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\mid z_{1}=z_{2}^{2}\}\,,

(6.20)

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}

\displaystyle=\{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\mid z_{1}=0\}\,,

(6.21)

and study the homotopy group of the complex space
\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}})
, in which these surfaces have been removed. This will teach us how the monodromy group acts on Feynman integrals near this intersection, and which will allow us to establish Theorem
2
.

\gamma
*
z_{1}
0
z_{2}^{2}

\eta_{+}^{\prime}
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
z_{2}
-\sqrt{z_{1}}
\sqrt{z_{1}}
*
\gamma

Figure 10:

The paths
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}
,

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5391,0.543}\eta_{+}^{\prime}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.5391,0.2344,0.543}\eta_{-}^{\prime}}
generate the first homotopy group of

\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}))
. The path
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}
encircles both
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
while
\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}
only encircle
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
. The base point for the paths is indicated as
\vec{z}_{\star}=(1,0)
is marked as
*
. As the path
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}
is traversed in the complex
z_{1}
plane, the singularity at
z_{2}=\sqrt{z_{1}}
moves, as indicated on the right. After the full
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}
contour, the
\pm\sqrt{z_{1}}
branches of
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
have changed places.

The homotopy group

\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}))
is generated by three loops, which can be chosen to be
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
,
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
, and
\gamma
as depicted in Fig.
10
. There, it can be seen that
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
go around the algebraic branch points that occur at
\pm\sqrt{z_{1}}
in the
z_{2}
plane, which involves encircling just
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
, while
\gamma
encircles both
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
. In the figure, we have chosen the basepoint of these loops to be

\vec{z}_{\star}=(z_{1}^{\star},z_{2}^{\star})=(1,0)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}})
.

An important pair of relations hold among the loops
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
,
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
, and
\gamma
:

\displaystyle\gamma\circ\eta_{+}^{\prime}\circ\gamma^{-1}

\displaystyle=\eta_{-}^{\prime}\,,

(6.22)

\displaystyle\gamma\circ\eta_{-}^{\prime}\circ\gamma^{-1}

\displaystyle=\eta_{+}^{\prime}\,,

(6.23)

where our convention for the composition of loops is
39
39

39

Some authors use the opposite convention, which is known as the “topologist’s convention”. Our preference for the convention in Eq. (
6.2
) stems from the fact that monodromies act on integrals from the left.

(\alpha\circ\beta)(t)=\begin{cases}\beta(2t),&\qquad t\in[0,\frac{1}{2}],\\
\alpha(2t-1),&\qquad t\in[\frac{1}{2},1].\end{cases}

The relations in Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
) are hard to visualize because they involve the analytic structure of
\sqrt{z}
in
\mathbb{C}
in an essential way. Intuitively, the idea is that conjugation by
\gamma
swaps
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
by interchanging the two roots of
\sqrt{z_{1}}
.
As a result, if we want to encircle
\sqrt{z_{1}}
, we can either travel along the contour
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
, or we can first exchange the two algebraic roots using
\gamma
, encircle
\sqrt{z_{1}}
by travelling along
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
, and then swap the algebraic roots back using
\gamma^{-1}
. Together, the relations in Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
) imply that
\gamma\circ\gamma\circ\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}\circ\gamma^{-1}\circ\gamma^{-1}=\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}
.

One way to derive Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
) is by constructing explicit realizations of the loops
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
,
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
, and
\gamma
. To do that, we first write the loops as maps from
u\in[0,1]
to
(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}})
:

\gamma(u)=\Big(e^{2\pi iu},\,0\Big),\quad\eta_{+}^{\prime}(u)=\Big(1,\,1-e^{2\pi iu}\Big),\quad\eta_{-}^{\prime}(u)=\Big(1,\,e^{2\pi iu}-1\Big).

(6.24)

We then construct a map
\psi\colon[0,1]\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}})

between
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
by interpolating along
\gamma
:

\psi(t,u)=\Big(\gamma(t),\,\sqrt{\gamma(t)}\,\eta_{+}^{\prime}(u)\Big)=\Big(e^{2\pi it},\,e^{\pi it}(1-e^{2\pi iu})\Big).

(6.25)

This map satisfies
\psi(0,u)=\eta_{+}^{\prime}(u)
and
\psi(1,u)=\eta_{-}^{\prime}(u)
. However, since the basepoint changes along the path, this is not a proper homotopy of paths. We can construct such a homotopy, in which the basepoint remains fixed, by conjugating by
\gamma
:

\Omega(t,u)=\begin{cases}\gamma(\frac{2u}{t}),&\qquad u\in[0,\frac{t}{2}),\\
\psi(t,2u-t),&\qquad u\in[\frac{t}{2},\frac{1+t}{2}],\\
\gamma(\frac{2u-1-t}{1-t}),&\qquad u\in(\frac{1+t}{2},1].\end{cases}

(6.26)

This satisfies
\Omega(t,0)=\Omega(t,1)=(1,0)
, so the basepoint is fixed for all
t
. It also satisfies
\Omega(0,u)=\gamma\circ\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\Omega(1,u)=\eta_{-}^{\prime}\circ\gamma
, which proves Eq. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
).

*
\eta_{+}^{\prime}

\eta_{-}

\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}

Figure 11:
Two principal Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
with
G^{\kappa^{\prime}}\supset G^{\kappa}

intersect tangentially. Locally the intersection is described by a parabola
z_{1}=z_{2}^{2}
and a line
z_{1}=0
. The intersection is codimension two and it separates the real, non-complexified Pham loci into two regions, corresponding to all
\alpha\geqslant 0
and its complement. The
\alpha
-positive part is a branch hypersurface in the physical region.
The paths
\eta_{+}
and
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
are called simple because they only encircle one branch point, in contrast to
\gamma=\eta_{+}^{\prime}\circ\eta_{+}
, which is not simple.

In more general situations, more powerful technology is needed to prove relations like those in Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
). Such relations can be proven algebraically, as described in Ref.
pham2011singularities
, using the homotopy exact sequence of a fibration. In this approach, one would represent
\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}})
as a fibration of
\mathbb{C}\setminus\{-\sqrt{z_{1}},\sqrt{z_{1}}\}
of coordinate
z_{2}
over
\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}
of coordinate
z_{1}
. An exact sequence for the homotopy of fibrations relates
\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}\cup\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}))
to
\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{-\sqrt{z_{1}},\sqrt{z_{1}}\})
and
\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\})
. The homotopy group
\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{-\sqrt{z_{1}},\sqrt{z_{1}}\})
is generated by the loops
\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}
, while
\pi_{1}(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\})
is generated by
\gamma
. This approach is described in more detail in appendix
F
.

Now that we have derived the relations in Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
), we can draw out their implications for Feynman integrals. But first, let us be precise about the relation between the monodromies of Feynman integrals (or more generally on absorption integrals) and the elements of the first homotopy group of
{\mathcal{S}}(G_{0})
.
The action of the elements in the homotopy group on these integrals is given by the Picard–Lefschetz theorem; that is, the action of the elements
\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}
on the Feynman integral
I_{G}(p)
correspond precisely to computing monodromies around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
. However, because
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
are not equivalent, we need to be more precise about which path we mean when we talk about the monodromy. For concreteness, we define the monodromy to be the
‘
+
’ contour:
\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\equiv\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}
.

The element that computes a monodromy around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
cannot be any of
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
,
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
, or
\gamma
, since the first two only encircle
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
, while the last one encircles both
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
. In particular,
\gamma
goes around the intersection point at
z_{1}=z_{2}=0
, and therefore, according to the terminology of Ref.
pham2011singularities
, is not a
simple loop
.
Conversely, the loops
\eta_{+}^{\prime}
and
\eta_{-}^{\prime}
that encircle the
z_{2}>0
and
z_{2}<0
branches of
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
are simple loops. We can define a similar pair of simple loops
\eta_{\pm}
that encircle the variety
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
using the relations

\gamma=\eta_{+}^{\prime}\circ\eta_{+}=\eta_{-}^{\prime}\circ\eta_{-}\,.

(6.27)

These loops are depicted in Fig.
11
, where one can see that these relations hold simply by contour composition. This contrasts with the relations in Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
), which required understanding the analytic structure of
\sqrt{z}
in
\mathbb{C}
. Indeed, the requirement that the Pham loci intersect tangentially was essential for Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
) to hold, while Eq. (
6.27
) holds even for a transversal intersection.

Note that we have implicitly chosen a convention in which the loop
\gamma
is equivalent to traversing the loops
\eta_{\pm}
before
\eta_{\pm}^{\prime}
in Eq. (
6.27
). In principle, we could have instead adopted the opposite order, and the equalities
\gamma=\eta_{+}\circ\eta_{+}^{\prime}=\eta_{-}\circ\eta_{-}^{\prime}
. However, a moment’s thought shows that this choice would conflict with the definition of the bubble absorption integral above the triangle threshold by analytic continuation through the upper complex plane. We also adopt a convention in which the monodromy around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
is given by the action of
\eta_{+}
, rather than
\eta_{-}
. That is,
\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\equiv\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}
.

Now, let us consider the action of the elements of the monodromy group on a generic Feynman integral
I_{G}(p)
. Combining Eq. (
6.27
) with Eqs. (
6.22
) and (
6.23
), we further have that

\gamma=\eta_{+}^{\prime}\circ\eta_{+}=\eta_{-}^{\prime}\circ\eta_{-}=\eta_{+}\circ\eta_{-}^{\prime}=\eta_{-}\circ\eta_{+}^{\prime}\,.

(6.28)

We can therefore write,

Theorem 3

(Pham)
.

If two Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
are of codimension one and intersect tangentially, then their sequential monodromies, in a small neighborhood of their intersection and away from other singularities, satisfy:

\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}I_{G}(p)=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}^{\prime}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}}I_{G}(p)=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}^{\prime}}I_{G}(p)=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}I_{G}(p)\,.

(6.29)

Note, in particular, that the monodromies on one side of the intersection do not commute (that is,
\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\neq\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}
). Moreover, while we have motivated Theorem
6.29
by studying principal Pham loci, we highlight that this theorem follows just from the properties of the local fundamental group close to the intersection of the two loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. Thus, we do not have to require that these loci are principal or in the physical region for this result to hold.
However, hierarchically-related singularities of type
S_{1}^{+}
constitute a physically-interesting set of cases where this theorem implies. For instance, all one-loop singularities are of
S_{1}^{+}
type, and the relation in Theorem
6.29
was used to construct the monodromy group for one-loop integrals in Ref.
Ponzano:1970ch
.

Next, let us look at what further constraints can be derived if we specialize to the physical region. To do this, we take the integration cycle for
I_{G}(p)
to be the physical one—namely, over real loop momenta, except for small deformations when required to avoid singularities, for which we can use the prescription detailed in Sec.
3.6
. We then know that the monodromy of
I_{G}(p)
vanishes around the part of
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
in which
\alpha_{e}<0
for any edge
e
. Since the Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
meet tangentially, one of the Feynman parameters of
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
changes sign at the intersection point where
z_{1}=z_{2}=0
.
For example, in the case of the triangle diagram, the line
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
corresponds to the bubble singularity, in which
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0
and
\alpha_{3}=0
, while the parabola
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
corresponds to the triangle singularity with
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0
. However, the remaining Feynman parameter
\alpha_{3}
is positive only positive on one branch of the locus
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
, since it flips sign at the point of intersection
z_{1}=z_{2}=0
.
Thus, we have that
\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}^{\prime}}I_{G}(p)=I_{G}(p)
.
This allows us to write

\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}^{\prime}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\;I_{G}(p)=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\circ\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{-}^{\prime}}\;I_{G}(p)=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}\;I_{G}(p)\,.

(6.30)

Hence, on the physical sheet, in a physical region where the triangle singularity is principal, we have

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\Big)I_{G}(p)=\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}(p)\,,

(6.31)

where we have made use of our adopted conventions, in which
\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}=\mathscr{M}_{\eta_{+}}
and
\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}=\mathscr{M}_{\eta^{\prime}_{+}}
. This proves Theorem
2
.

As a first example that illustrates Theorem

, we return to the triangle integral

), additional insight can be gleaned by studying the on-shell surfaces that are relevant to this case, and the

Let us first solve for the leading singularity of the triangle (as is done, for instance, in Ref.

). In the
y_{ij}
variables in Eq. (

), the Landau equations are given by

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}m_{1}-\alpha_{2}m_{2}y_{12}-\alpha_{3}m_{3}y_{13}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(6.32)

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}m_{1}y_{23}-\alpha_{2}m_{2}-\alpha_{3}m_{3}y_{13}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(6.33)

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}m_{1}y_{23}-\alpha_{2}m_{2}y_{12}-\alpha_{3}m_{3}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(6.34)

These have non-trivial solution when
D=0
, where we recall that
D
was defined in Eq. (
4.8
). On the support of this solution, the three Landau equations above become redundant, and we can deduce the relations

\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\alpha_{3}}=\frac{m_{3}}{m_{1}}\frac{y_{13}+y_{12}y_{23}}{1-y_{12}^{2}},\qquad\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{3}}=\frac{m_{3}}{m_{2}}\frac{y_{23}+y_{12}y_{13}}{1-y_{12}^{2}}\,,

(6.35)

from the first two equations.

y_{23}
y_{13}

The Pham loci for the triangle diagram in three dimensions. The yellow surface depicts the
D=0
surface where the triangle singularity occurs, while the blue, green, and red planes depict the locations of the bubble singularities at

. On the right, we show in yellow the

The location of the bubble singularities can be determined by setting one of the Feynman parameters to zero. For
example, setting
\alpha_{3}=0
contracts the
q_{3}
line to a point. The remaining
Landau equations are then

\displaystyle m_{1}\alpha_{1}-m_{2}\alpha_{2}y_{12}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(6.36)

\displaystyle-m_{1}\alpha_{1}y_{12}+m_{2}\alpha_{2}

\displaystyle=0\,.

(6.37)

The only nontrivial solution to this pair of equations is given by
y_{12}^{2}=1
.
On this locus,
m_{1}\alpha_{1}=m_{2}\alpha_{2}y_{12}
, which implies that the

\alpha
-positive region corresponds to the
y_{12}=1
branch.

In Fig.
12
, we show the on-shell surface for the triangle
(D=0)
and the bubble contractions of the triangle (
y_{ij}^{2}=1
).
There, we see that there are four regions where one can reach the
D=0
surface. The first corresponds to the region in which
-1<y_{12},y_{23},y_{13}<1
, while the remaining three regions are determined by one of the three variables being less than
-1
, and the remaining two to be greater than 1. Let us specialize to the region in which
y_{13},y_{23}>1
and
y_{12}<-1
. In this region,
1-y_{12}^{2}<0
, so from Eq. (
6.35
) we can read off the
\alpha
-positivity conditions to be
y_{13}+y_{12}y_{23}<0
and
y_{23}+y_{12}y_{13}<0
. On the surface
D=0
, these
constraints reduce to
y_{12}+y_{13}<0
and
y_{12}+y_{23}<0
. The bubble singularity at
y_{23}=1

intersects with the triangle singularity on the line
y_{12}+y_{13}=0
. Since we are interested
in the two directions that are transverse to this line, let us fix
y_{12}
to
some fiducial value, and introduce a coordinate

z_{1}
that points in the
y_{23}
direction and a coordinate
z_{2}
that points in the
y_{13}
direction. More precisely, we define

\displaystyle z_{1}=2(y_{12}^{2}-1)(y_{23}-1)\,,\qquad z_{2}=y_{12}+y_{13}\,.

(6.38)

These definitions are chosen so that the intersection of the bubble and triangle singularities occurs at
z_{1}=z_{2}=0
, and so the leading term in the expansion of
z_{2}
around this intersection point has unit coefficient (as we will see momentarily). In these variables, the line
y_{23}=1
is given by
z_{1}=0
, while the
D=0
curve becomes

\displaystyle z_{1}

\displaystyle=2(1-y_{12}^{2})\left(1+\sqrt{(1-y_{12}^{2})(1-(y_{12}-z_{2})^{2})}+y_{12}(z_{2}-y_{12})\right)

(6.39)

\displaystyle=z_{2}^{2}+\frac{y_{12}}{y_{12}^{2}-1}z_{2}^{3}+\mathcal{O}(z_{2}^{4})\,.

(6.40)

This is form we expect this curve to take (at leading order) from our analysis in Sec.
6.1
. In terms of
z_{2}
, the
\alpha
-positive condition becomes

z_{2}=y_{12}+y_{13}<0
. These regions and surfaces are shown on the right side of Fig.
12
.

(6.41)

Momentum conservation reads

\displaystyle p_{1}^{\mu}+p_{2}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=q_{2}^{\mu}+q_{3}^{\mu}+q_{4}^{\mu},

(6.42)

\displaystyle p_{4}^{\mu}-p_{3}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=-q_{1}^{\mu}+q_{3}^{\mu}+q_{4}^{\mu},

(6.43)

\displaystyle p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=q_{1}^{\mu}+q_{2}^{\mu}.

(6.44)

Landau singularities

The Landau loop equations for the ice cream cone diagram read

\displaystyle\alpha_{3}q_{3}^{\mu}-\alpha_{4}q_{4}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=0,

(6.45)

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}q_{1}^{\mu}-\alpha_{2}q_{2}^{\mu}+\alpha_{4}q_{4}^{\mu}

\displaystyle=0.

(6.46)

Squaring the first equation, we find
\alpha_{3}^{2}q_{3}^{2}=\alpha_{4}^{2}q_{4}^{2}
. Using the on-shell conditions and the constraint that
\alpha_{3},\alpha_{4}\geqslant 0
, we have
\alpha_{3}m_{3}=\alpha_{4}m_{4}
. This implies that
q_{3}^{\mu}=\frac{m_{3}}{m_{3}+m_{4}}(q_{3}^{\mu}+q_{4}^{\mu})
and
q_{4}^{\mu}=\frac{m_{4}}{m_{3}+m_{4}}(q_{3}^{\mu}+q_{4}^{\mu})
. The second Landau loop equation then becomes

\alpha_{1}q_{1}^{\mu}-\alpha_{2}q_{2}^{\mu}+\frac{\alpha_{4}m_{4}}{m_{3}+m_{4}}(q_{3}^{\mu}+q_{4}^{\mu})=0.

(6.47)

Codimension-two momentum configuration

For special values of the external kinematics, the leading ice cream cone singularity becomes codimension-two (the analysis of this codimension-two situation is proposed as an exercise in Sec. I.3.2 of Ref.
pham
). Let us take the external kinematics to be such that the external linear combinations of momenta
p_{1}^{\mu}+p_{2}^{\mu}
and
p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}
(and by momentum conservation,
p_{3}^{\mu}-p_{4}^{\mu}
) are collinear. In this configuration, the space of external kinematics becomes one-dimensional and each of the Landau loop equations contribute one constraint. Hence, only two of the four
\alpha
are determined and we end up with a codimension-two singularity.

When the three momenta
p_{1}^{\mu}+p_{2}^{\mu}
,
p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}
, and
p_{3}^{\mu}-p_{4}^{\mu}
are collinear, the map between the components of these momenta and the Mandelstam invariants that describe this process is not regular. To see this, consider the differential
\beta_{1}d(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}+\beta_{2}d(p_{3}-p_{4})^{2}+\beta_{3}d(p_{5}+p_{6})^{2}
. One can find values for
\beta_{i}
such that it vanishes when the three momenta
p_{1}^{\mu}+p_{2}^{\mu}
,
p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}
and
p_{3}^{\mu}-p_{4}^{\mu}
are collinear. As described in Ref.
pham
, the inverse map from Mandelstam invariants to components of momenta will then not be well-defined. As a consequence, the form taken by the Pham locus in the neighborhood of special kinematic points where the space of kinematics is lower-dimensional depends on the coordinates one works in terms of. When described in Mandelstam invariants, we find that these lower-dimensional configurations correspond to points. In terms of components of momenta, they correspond to curves.

Ice cream cone variety in terms of momentum components

To illustrate how this works in detail, we take all the masses to be equal to
m
, and work in units where
m=1
. We also work in light-cone coordinates, in which
q_{i}^{\mu}=(q_{i}^{+},q_{i}^{-})
, with
q_{i}^{-}=1/{q_{i}^{+}}
and
q_{i}^{2}=q_{i}^{+}q_{i}^{-}
(since we have three independent external Mandelstam variables for the ice cream cone, we can go to a frame in which the transverse components vanish in light-cone coordinates, so we omit them for simplicity). We can choose our external kinematics to be such that
p_{1}^{\mu}+p_{2}^{\mu}=(u,v)
and
p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}=(w,w)
.
The positivity of energy implies
u+v>0
and
w>0
. The reason for this choice of parametrization of the
p_{5}^{\mu}+p_{6}^{\mu}
components is that the on-shell and momentum-conservation conditions at that vertex can be solved by
q_{1}=(x,x^{-1})
and
q_{2}=(x^{-1},x)
, with
w=x+x^{-1}
. Since the masses have been chosen to be equal, the bubble Landau loop equation implies that
\alpha_{3}=\alpha_{4}
and
q_{3}^{\mu}=q_{4}^{\mu}
. Hence, a simple parametrization of the internal momenta is provided by

\displaystyle q_{3}^{\mu}=q_{4}^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}(u-x^{-1},v-x).

(6.53)

The on-shell condition for
q_{3}
is then
(v-x)(u-x^{-1})=4
and can be parameterized by
v=x+2y^{-1}
and
u=x^{-1}+2y
. Hence, we have found a parametrization in terms of
x
and
y
which solve the on-shell conditions as

\displaystyle q_{1}^{\mu}=(x,x^{-1}),\qquad q_{2}^{\mu}=(x^{-1},x),\qquad q_{3}^{\mu}=q_{4}^{\mu}=(y,y^{-1}).

(6.54)

The two components of the remaining Landau loop equation are

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}x-\alpha_{2}x^{-1}+\alpha_{4}y=0,

(6.55)

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}x^{-1}-\alpha_{2}x+\alpha_{4}y^{-1}=0.

(6.56)

These always admit a solution, so they do not impose additional constraints on the external kinematics.

We have now obtained a rational parameterization of the codimension-one Pham locus associated with the ice cream cone Landau singularity, in which all Feynman parameters are non-vanishing. This parameterization is

\displaystyle f\colon\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{3},

(6.57)

\displaystyle(x,y)\mapsto(u,v,w)=(x^{-1}+2y,x+2y^{-1},x+x^{-1}).

(6.58)

We can eliminate the variables
x
and
y
to express the Pham locus by the equation

u^{2}v^{2}-u^{2}vw-uv^{2}w+uvw^{2}+u^{2}-8uv+v^{2}+3uw+3vw+9=0\,.

(6.59)

Note that this Pham locus has a self-intersection singularity: there is a one-dimensional locus where one obtains the same values
(u,v,w)
for
two
different values of
(x,y)
. Indeed, given values of
x
and
y
such that
y-y^{-1}=2(x-x^{-1})
, we have that both
(x,y)
and
(x^{-1},y^{-1})
map to the same value of
(u,v,w)
.

For unit masses, the two-loop sunrise Pham locus
\mathcal{P}_{{\hbox to7.43pt{\vbox to5.21pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.71419pt\lower-2.6061pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0,0,0.5469}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}
{{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}}{{{}}{{}}}{}{{}}{}{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -4.72 0 C -2.88 -3.19 2.88 -3.19 4.72 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope
{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}{}
{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{{}}
{{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}}{{{}}{{}}}{}{{}}{}{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -4.72 0 C -2.88 3.19 2.88 3.19 4.72 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -4.72 0 L 4.72 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}
corresponding to
\alpha_{1}=0
is given by
(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=9
, or
uv=9
, and it can be parameterized by
(u,w)\mapsto(u,\frac{9}{u},w)
. The bubble Pham locus corresponds to
\alpha_{3}=\alpha_{4}=0
, and is given by
(p_{5}+p_{6})^{2}=4
, or
w^{2}=4
. It can be parameterized by
(u,v)\mapsto(u,v,2)
.
The ice cream cone singularity intersects the two-loop sunrise singularity in a curve parameterized by
x\mapsto(3x^{-1},3x,x+x^{-1})
. The ice cream cone intersects the bubble singularity in a curve parameterized by
y\mapsto(1+2y,1+2y^{-1},2)
. The bubble and two-loop sunrise intersect in a curve defined by
w=2
and
uv=9
. All three Pham loci intersect at the point
(u,v,w)=(3,3,2)
, which corresponds to
x=y=1
.

Fig.
14
shows the ice cream cone Pham locus (given by the parabolic surface), and the bubble and sunrise Pham loci (which correspond to planes). For visualization purposes, we have changed variables from
v
to
{\tilde{v}}=\frac{1}{v}
. This makes the sunrise Pham locus the plane
u=9\tilde{v}
. The ice cream cone surface intersects both the sunrise and bubble surfaces tangentially, while the sunrise and bubble surfaces intersect each other transversally.

Not all the points of this locus correspond to positive
\alpha
. Solving for these variables, we find that, projectively,

\displaystyle(\alpha_{1}:\alpha_{2}:\alpha_{4})

\displaystyle=((1-x^{2}y^{2})x:(x^{2}-y^{2})x:(x^{4}-1)y),

\displaystyle(\alpha_{3}:\alpha_{4})

\displaystyle=(1:1)\,.

(6.61)

The parameterization of the Pham locus from Eq. (
6.59
) is given in terms of components of the external momenta, in a special frame parametrized by
(u,v,w)
. As we saw in Eq. (
6.48
), the Pham locus looks different in terms of the Mandelstam variables
(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=uv
,
(p_{3}-p_{4})^{2}=(w-u)(w-v)
, and
(p_{5}+p_{6})^{2}=w^{2}
. In the
(u,v,w)
parameterization the locus has a singularity of Whitney umbrella type,
40
40

40

A Whitney umbrella is a singularity of a surface in the neighborhood of which the surface can be represented either by an equation
x^{2}-y^{2}z=0
or, equivalently, by a parameterization
(u,v)\mapsto(x,y,z)=(uv,u,v^{2})
. In this parameterization the surface is ruled by a family of lines; for any fixed value
v
we have a line in the
(x,y)
plane at
z=v^{2}
, defined by
u\mapsto(x,y)=(uv,u)
. In the same plane, we have a line corresponding to
-v
. These lines intersect at
(x,y)=(0,0)
. It follows that the surface has a self-intersection along the
z
axis; at
z=0
the two lines become coincident. The singularity at
(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)
is called a
pinch point
singularity. The Whitney umbrella also has a “handle” along the
z
axis defined by
x=y=0
. See Fig.
14
for a sketch of this singularity, but note that in that figure the surface far away from the singularity looks different (in particular it is not ruled by lines anymore), due to the higher-order polynomial terms that go beyond the ones described above.
while in the Mandelstam parameterization it has a conical singularity at a point.

We associate a
d

X_{c}
to every fundamental loop

•

These vectors have to satisfy the constraints

(6.64)

for all

. This is the constraint that the

belong to the

.

•

We define a quadratic form

A(X)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c_{1},c_{2}\in\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa)\\
e\in E(\ker\kappa)\end{subarray}}\alpha_{e}b_{c_{1}e}b_{c_{2}e}X_{c_{1}}\cdot X_{c_{2}}.

(6.65)

The singularity is
S
-type if the quadratic form

, restricted to the kernel of the tangent map (defined above), is positive or negative definite for positive values of the
\alpha_{e}
.

42

Here we take the ice cream cone integral in more than two dimensions so the vectors
X_{1}
and
X_{2}
can exist. In four dimensions the integral contains a logarithmic ultraviolet divergence from a sub-bubble and this complicates the analysis.
Then the quadratic form becomes

A(X)=X_{1}^{2}.

(6.69)

In particular, this does not depend on
X_{2}
anymore so not only is the quadratic form not definite, but it is in fact
degenerate
. Therefore, this singularity cannot be understood in terms of quadratic pinches anymore. In this case a generalization of the Picard–Lefschetz formula has to be applied which instead of vanishing spheres involves generalizations called Pham–Brieskorn spheres (see Refs.
pham1965formules
;
MR198497
). For further discussions on the bubble-like singularity, see Refs.
Kawai1976DiscontinuityFA
;
Kawai:1981fs
;
Honda2014OnTG
.

7
Non-hierarchical Sequential Discontinuities

In Sec.
6
we analyzed situations in which we had two principal Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
that were hierarchically related, so that
G\twoheadrightarrow G^{\kappa^{\prime}}\twoheadrightarrow G^{\kappa}\twoheadrightarrow G_{0}
.
In such cases, we found that the value of the discontinuity around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
was unaffected by whether or not one computed a discontinuity around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
first.
In this section, we consider situations in which different types of relations hold for pairs of Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
. These relations will take the form of double discontinuities that are forced to vanish,

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\Big)I_{G}(p)=0\,,

(7.1)

or double discontinuities that commute,

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\Big)I_{G}(p)=\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}(p)\,.

(7.2)

We will also be able to formulate a graphical condition for when these relations hold.

Actually, we already know situations in which the relation in Eq. (
7.1
) holds.
By Theorem
1
, the absorption integral
A_{G}^{\kappa}(p)=\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}}\Big)I_{G}(p)
can only have singularities on Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
when
{\kappa^{\prime}}
dominates
\kappa
. Thus, when
{\kappa^{\prime}}
does not dominate
\kappa
, the sequential relation in Eq. (
7.1
) immediately follows. Conversely, we know that when
{\kappa^{\prime}}
dominates
\kappa
, the sequential discontinuity does
not
generically vanish when
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
are principal loci; it is equal to the discontinuity around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
, as shown in Sec.
6
. However, in this section, we will go beyond these cases by considering pairs of Pham loci that are not hierarchically related.

It is worth first commenting on why double discontinuities with respect to non-hierarchical Pham loci can be nontrivial, as this seems to contradict Theorem
1
. For instance, in the case of relations taking the form of Eq. (
7.2
), Theorem
1
must be satisfied on both sides of the equation. This simultaneously requires that
{\kappa^{\prime}}
dominates
\kappa
on the left side while
\kappa
dominates
{\kappa^{\prime}}
on the right side, which can only be the case if
\kappa={\kappa^{\prime}}
. This would seem to restrict Eq. (
7.2
) to cases in which it is tautological.
All is not lost, however, because Pham loci can have different branches; recall that their definition requires all the lines in
\ker\kappa
to be on shell, but puts no restrictions on the values of the associated
\alpha_{e}
parameters, except that they cannot all be zero.
Thus, like in the example in Sec.
6.4
, we can consider subspaces of these loci where some
\alpha_{e}
are zero, even though the associated edges are on-shell. For example, if we take a one-vertex reducible diagram

7.1
Transversal Intersections

Just as the situation we considered in Sec.
6
had a geometric interpretation as the Pham loci intersecting tangentially, there is a geometric interpretation of having pairs of loci that intersect transversally: when the intersection of Pham loci is transversal, the discontinuities commute.
The general statement was proven by Pham:

Theorem 4

(Pham)
.

If two Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
intersect transversally, then their sequential discontinuities, in a small neighborhood of their intersection and away from other singularities, commute:

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}(p)=\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}(p)\,.

(7.7)

Note that this theorem does not put any conditions on the Pham loci involved in this intersection: they can be of any codimension, and do not have to be principal,
\alpha
-positive, or in the physical region. Of course, in many situations both sides of this equation will vanish, but the fact that the discontinuities commute only requires transversality.

z_{2}
z_{1}
*
\eta^{\prime}
\eta_{+}
\eta_{-}
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}

Figure 16:
Two Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
that intersect
transversally. Locally, the intersection is described by the surfaces
z_{1}=0
and
z_{2}=0
. The two cycles around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
labeled
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5391,0.543}{\eta_{+}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.5469}{\eta_{-}}}
are homotopically equivalent: one can simply slip the loop over the intersection by giving
z_{2}
a small imaginary part at the crossing. Thus, at a transversal intersection, the local homotopy group is Abelian:
{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}\eta^{\prime}}
, the monodromy around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
, commutes with
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5391,0.543}{\eta_{+}}}\approx{\color[rgb]{0,0,0.5469}{\eta_{-}}}
.

It is easy to see why the transversality condition is sufficient for concluding that discontinuities commute. Let us assume both Pham loci are codimension one (otherwise the corresponding discontinuities are zero and their commutation is trivial). When these surfaces intersect transversally, we can always choose coordinates for
\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}\cup P_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})
in the neighborhood of the intersection in which
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
corresponds to the surface
z_{1}=0
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
corresponds to the surface
z_{2}=0
. Then the space itself factorizes, so
\mathbb{C}^{2}\setminus(\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}\cup P_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})=\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}
. Thus, the monodromies around each singularity are totally independent of the other. We visualize this in Fig.
16
, in which the two monodromies
\eta_{+}
and
\eta_{-}
are homotopically equivalent. The monodromy
\eta^{\prime\prime}
around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
thus commutes with the monodromy
\eta^{\prime}
around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
:

\eta^{\prime}\circ\eta^{\prime\prime}=\eta^{\prime\prime}\circ\eta^{\prime}.

(7.8)

As a result, computing the corresponding discontinuities in either order gives the same result.

7.2
Compatibility of Contractions

While Theorem
7.7
does not place any requirements on the pair of Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
beyond their transversal intersection, we now turn our attention to a stronger result that can be established for principal Pham loci in physical regions.
43
43

43

Note that this implies that we only consider cases in which the kernels of
\kappa
and
{\kappa^{\prime}}
are neither disconnected graphs or bouquets of graphs (one-vertex reducible). In Sec.
8
we will consider kernels which are disconnected graphs.
To do so, we first note that, given any such pair of principal loci, one can formulate a Pham diagram of the type shown on the left side of Fig.
15
; one just needs to find a graph
G^{\kappa}
which contracts to both
G^{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
G^{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. However, in the generic case, there will be no special relation between the kernels of the four contractions
{\kappa^{\prime}}
,
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
,
\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
, and
\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
.

The Pham diagram for the double-bubble example on the right side of Fig.
15
has the special property that
\ker\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}=\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\ker\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}=\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. When both of these relations are satisfied, the contractions
\kappa
and
{\kappa^{\prime}}
are said to be
compatible

pham
. If either is not satisfied, we say that these contractions are
incompatible
.
When a pair of contractions are compatible, one can take
\ker\kappa=\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}\oplus\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
, meaning
\kappa
is a fiber product of
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. The general result that holds in this situation, again proven by Pham, is:

Theorem 5

(Pham)
.

Assume we have two principal Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
that intersect transversally. Then, for generic masses,

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}(p)=0\,,

(7.9)

if
\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
are incompatible, and
p
is in the physical region.

We first explore this notion of compatibility in an example, then outline a general derivation of this result.

y_{ij}=\pm 1
. The surfaces corresponding to each of these bubble contractions intersect transversally, as illustrated in Fig.
12

(7.10)

Writing
q_{1}^{\mu}=k^{\mu}
and
q_{2}^{\mu}=p_{3}^{\mu}-k^{\mu}
, the Landau equations require

k^{\mu}=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}p_{3}^{\mu},\quad k^{2}=m_{1}^{2},\quad(k-p_{3})^{2}=m_{2}^{2},

(7.11)

which have the solution
p_{3}^{2}=(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}
. In the rest frame of
p_{3}^{\mu}
, Eq. (
7.11
) imposes
k^{\mu}=(m_{1},0)
and
p_{3}^{\mu}=(m_{1}+m_{2},0)
, which corresponds to a two-parameter, and therefore codimension-one, solution in the space of external momenta.
The discontinuity around the threshold at

{{}{}}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0,0,0}{}{}{}{}{{}}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -39.37 0 L -17.07 0}{fill:none} {{}{{}}{}{}{{}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-12.3332pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 7.22 0 C 5.08 0.4 1.61 1.61 -0.8 3.01 L -0.8 -3.01 C 1.61 -1.61 5.08 -0.4 7.22 0}{stroke:none} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

(7.12)

The Landau equations for this contraction are

k^{\mu}=\frac{\alpha_{3}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{1}^{\prime}+\alpha_{3}^{\prime}}p_{2}^{\mu},\quad k^{2}=m_{1}^{2},\quad(k-p_{2})^{2}=m_{3}^{2}.

(7.13)

In the rest frame of
p_{2}
, Eq. (
7.13
) imposes
k^{\mu}=(m_{1},0)
and
p_{2}^{\mu}=(m_{1}+m_{3},0)
, which is another codimension-one solution.

By constructing the appropriate Pham diagram, one can check that the pair of contractions corresponding to
p_{3}^{2}=(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}
and
p_{2}^{2}=(m_{1}+m_{3})^{2}
is incompatible, and thus by Theorem
5
we expect the corresponding double discontinuity of the triangle integral to vanish. To see that this is indeed what happens, we recall that computing a discontinuity with respect to the
p_{2}^{2}
threshold after computing a discontinuity with respect to the
p_{3}^{2}
threshold requires maintaining the on-shell condition
(k-p_{3})^{2}-m_{2}^{2}=0
when the second discontinuity is computed. This provides an extra constraint on the momentum
p_{3}^{\mu}
that must be imposed in addition to the Landau equations in Eq (
7.13
), which leaves just a one-parameter family of solutions. This encodes a codimension-two surface in
{\mathcal{S}}(G_{0})
, and therefore the monodromy around this surface will vanish. Stated differently, there is no
p_{2}^{2}
normal threshold of the absorption integral
A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}
, in accordance with Theorem
5
. A similar result holds when the discontinuities are computed in the opposite order.

In contrast, we know from Sec.
6
that the absorption integral
A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}
has a nonzero discontinuity with respect to the triangle singularity at
D=0
. In this case, the Landau equations for the triangle also give a codimension-one surface, but again we must impose the on-shell conditions associated with the bubble diagram in (
7.10
). However, because all the edges in the bubble are also in the triangle, they are already on shell; there is no new constraint. Thus, the solution space will remain codimension-one and the monodromy can be nonzero. Indeed, the bubble absorption integral for the three-dimensional triangle diagram in Eq. (
4.12
) only has a singularity at
D=0
and not at
y_{ij}^{2}=1
, in accordance with the sequential-discontinuity analysis.

Another way to understand this result is to recall that the absorption integral that gives the discontinuity with respect to
p_{3}^{2}
has the form given in Eq. (
4.11
):

A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}=(2\pi i)^{2}\int_{\partial_{1}\partial_{2}e_{12}}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}k}{(\mathrm{d}s_{1}\wedge\mathrm{d}s_{2})s_{3}},

(7.14)

where
s_{i}=q_{i}^{2}-m_{i}^{2}
.
Here we have a function
s_{3}
defined on the vanishing sphere
\partial_{1}\partial_{2}e_{12}
where
s_{1}=s_{2}=0
. We want to know when the restriction to
s_{3}=0
of the projection to external kinematics has a critical point. In other words, we want to know when
\mathrm{d}s_{3}|_{s_{1}=s_{2}=0}=0
when restricted to fixed external kinematics. This is a constrained extremization problem. To make it unconstrained we introduce Lagrange multipliers and we end up with the condition

\mathrm{d}s_{3}+\alpha_{1}\mathrm{d}s_{1}+\alpha_{2}\mathrm{d}s_{2}=0,

(7.15)

which is equivalent to the triangle Landau equation. In other words, the only codimension-one singularity of the bubble absorption integral is on the triangle singularity.

Sketch of a Proof of Theorem
5

Let us now outline a derivation of Theorem
5
. We start by considering an integral of the form

I_{G}=\int_{h}\omega\,,

(7.16)

where the integration domain
h
lives in
{\mathcal{E}}(G)
, which we recall denotes the space of momentum-conserving internal and external momentum of the graph
G
.
The discontinuity of
I_{G}
with respect to a principal Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
gives an absorption integral

A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}=\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}=\int_{\chi^{\prime}}\omega^{\prime}\,,

(7.17)

where
\omega^{\prime}
is an integrand of the form seen in Eq. (
3.63
), and
\chi^{\prime}
is the vanishing sphere whose construction was described in Sec.
3.3
.

The contour
\chi^{\prime}
forms a fiber over
{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
in
{\mathcal{E}}(G)
. In particular, all that is really relevant for computing this monodromy is the space
\mathcal{E}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
, since no edges other than those of
\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
participate in the Landau equations. Thus, we can define
\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}\subset{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})\subset\mathcal{E}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
as the restriction of the vanishing sphere to this smaller space. Equivalently, it is the fiber over the basepoint
p
in this space, which can be defined as the inverse image of the projection map
\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}\colon{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})\to{\mathcal{S}}(G_{0})
. That is,
\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}=\pi_{\kappa^{\prime}}^{-1}(p)
. With this definition we can rewrite

A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}=\int_{\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\int_{h^{\prime}}\omega^{\prime}\,,

(7.18)

where now
h^{\prime}
includes whatever additional integrations are in Eq. (
7.17
) but not in the new contour
{\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}}
.

Now let us consider computing the monodromy of
A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}
around
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. Following the Picard–Lefschetz approach, this monodromy pushes the integration contour out of the way of this singularity. But one can ask: does it deform the
\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}
contour, the
h^{\prime}
contour, or both? Because
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
intersect transversally, near the intersection the monodromies commute. This implies that
\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}
is unaffected by the second monodromy.
Thus the monodromy operator can be passed through the outer integral, and we have

\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}\Big)\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big)I_{G}=\int_{\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}\Big)\int_{h^{\prime}}\omega^{\prime}\,.

(7.19)

On the other hand, we can ask more generally for which Pham loci
\mathcal{P}
the integral

\int_{\chi_{\kappa^{\prime}}}\Big({\mathds{1}}-\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{P}}\Big)\int_{h^{\prime}}\omega^{\prime}

(7.20)

will be nonzero. As with Lemma
1
, these loci are critical points of the projection map from one on-shell space to another. In this case, since the first monodromy takes place on a fiber over
{\mathcal{S}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
, the edges in
\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
are on-shell on both sides of the map. That is, the singularities are on Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}}
for any
{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}:G^{\kappa}\twoheadrightarrow G^{\kappa^{\prime}}
.

We are almost done. We are still interested in the second discontinuity for
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
in Eq. (
7.19
), where the loop equations for the loops in
\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
are satisfied. But as stated above, the only possible nonzero discontinuities will be for loci
\mathcal{P}_{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}
in which the loop equations for the loops in
\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}
are satisfied. Therefore, we must be able to find a
{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}
for which
\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}=\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
.
Since the discontinuities commute, by Theorem
7.7
, we must also be able to find a
{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}}
for which
\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}}=\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
.
Therefore, the contractions must be compatible for the sequential discontinuity to be nonzero. That completes the sketch of the proof. More details can be found in Sec. II.3.4 and Sec. I.3.3 of Ref.
pham
.

7.3
Compatibility of Landau Equations

We have defined a pair of contractions to be compatible when the horizontal and vertical kernels are equal in a Pham diagram. There is also a more direct algebraic way to understand the compatibility of pairs of discontinuities through the Landau equations. The claim is that:

Lemma 2
.

Suppose we have two contractions
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}

corresponding to a pair of codimension-one Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
such that neither contraction dominates the other.
Then, for generic masses, they are compatible if and only if one can solve both the Landau equations for
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
simultaneously.

When we can solve both sets of Landau equations simultaneously, we say that the
Landau equations are compatible
. A schematic diagram is shown in Fig.
17
.

\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
p_{1}
p_{2}
k

Figure 17:
Although two Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
may intersect transversally in the space formed by some external momenta, labeled as
p_{1}
and
p_{2}
, they do not necessarily intersect in the internal-variable space, schematically shown as
k
. When the discontinuity around
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
is given by Cutkosky’s formula, its integration contour
h^{\prime}
localizes close to the Landau-singularity solution in the space of loop momenta
k
. If the Landau-equation solution
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
also puts a constraint on the loop momentum
k
, the corresponding vanishing cell entering the Picard–Lefschetz theorem will generally not intersect the integration contour
h^{\prime}
.

Rather than prove this lemma directly, let us first state a related lemma from which Lemma
2
follows:

Lemma 3
.

Suppose we have a pair of compatible contractions
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
that describe two codimension-one Pham loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
. Then, for generic masses, the Landau diagram that describes the codimension-two Pham locus associated with the combined contraction
{\kappa^{\prime}}\circ{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}={\kappa^{\prime\prime}}\circ{\kappa^{\prime}}
factorizes into a pair of diagrams that separately describe the two loci
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
.

From this lemma, it follows that the only allowed sequential discontinuities that do not vanish according to Theorem
5
are those for which the Landau diagram for the codimension-two variety factorizes into a one-vertex reducible diagram, as depicted in Eq. (
7.4
).
Below, we will prove this lemma and consider an example in which this factorization property holds; for now, we just sketch how Lemma
2
is implied by Lemma
3
.

To show this, we first assume the pair of contractions
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
in Lemma
2
are compatible. Then, by Lemma
3
, the Landau diagram that describes the combined contraction
{\kappa^{\prime}}\circ{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
factorizes, and the kernels of
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
do not share any loop momenta. As a result, the two sets of Landau equations can be solved simultaneously. To establish the converse, let us now assume that the two contractions are incompatible, and therefore both involve some loop momentum
k_{c}
. Since by assumption neither contraction dominates the other, both
\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
must also involve at least one edge the other lacks. However, since
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
are both codimension-one, each of the critical points
p
these contractions describe corresponds to a unique solution for all the momenta
q_{e}^{\mu}
and
k_{c}^{\mu}
that appear in their kernel. For each point
p^{\star}
that exists within the intersection of
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
in the space of external momenta, the solutions for the loop momenta
k_{c}^{\mu}(p^{\star})
will generically be different, since the masses are assumed to be generic. Thus, when contractions are incompatible it is not generically possible to solve both sets of Landau equations simultaneously. This completes our proof.

We can use the fact that the Landau equations are compatible to gain a different, perhaps more physical, perspective on Theorem
5
.
Recall that the Picard–Lefschetz analysis from Sec.
3
takes place in an arbitrarily small region near the singular point we call the Leray bubble (as illustrated in Eq. (
3.38
)). The vanishing cell and the relevant part of the integration contour for computing the discontinuity are both within the Leray bubble. For
{\kappa^{\prime}}
this Leray bubble lives in
{\mathcal{E}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime}})
, while for
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
this Leray bubble lives in
{\mathcal{E}}(G^{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})
. Both bubbles are subspaces of the space of internal and external momenta associated with the original graph
{\mathcal{E}}(G^{\kappa})
.
When two Landau equations are incompatible, the solution for
k_{c}(p^{\star})
at an intersection point
p^{\star}
are different functions of external momenta. Thus the Leray bubbles corresponding to
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
for
p
arbitrarily close to
p^{\star}
will not intersect in
{\mathcal{E}}(G^{\kappa})
. This means that the integration contour for
A_{G}^{\kappa^{\prime}}
will not intersect the vanishing cell for
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
, and vice versa. Therefore, in neither case is the contour of the absorption integral pinched by the second singularity, and therefore the sequential monodromy is zero. This provides another interpretation of Eq. (
7.19
).

For an even more direct proof of Theorem
5
, we can simply try to solve the Landau equations for
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
when the additional on-shell constraints for the edges in
\ker{\kappa^{\prime}}
are imposed, and the Landau diagram formed out of both contractions does not factorize. Since
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
is a codimension-one solution to the loop equations and the on-shell conditions encoded just by the contraction
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
, imposing additional on-shell constraints will make it codimension-two or higher in the space of external momenta. Thus, there can be no discontinuity.

7.4
Allowed Sequential Discontinuities

{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}
{\kappa^{\prime}}
{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}}
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}

Figure 18:
Pham diagram for the bow-tie integral, which describes one of the pairs of sequential discontinuities that can appear in the double-box integral.

Lemma
3
puts strong constraints on what sequences of discontinuities can occur in Feynman integrals that depend on generic masses. Namely, all possible sequential discontinuities are described by Landau diagrams that are
one-vertex reducible
, meaning they factorize into two or more diagrams if one vertex is removed. This property has the effect of factorizing the loop momentum dependence, so that each edge only depends on the loop momenta on the left or right side of the diagram, but not both. As a result, the corresponding Landau equations and Pham loci also trivially factorize. We now consider an example that illustrates this phenomenon, after which we will prove Lemma
3
.

(7.32)

subject to the usual caveats that the loci
\mathcal{P}_{\hbox to3.53pt{\vbox to4.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.4pt\lower-2.44849pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\hbox to3.53pt{\vbox to4.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 3.13148pt\lower-2.44849pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
{}{{}}{}
{}{}
{}{}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -3.78 -2.83 L -3.78 2.83 L 0 0 Z}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}
intersect transversally and do not overlap with other Pham loci.
This picture holds to all orders in perturbation theory, although for any particular perturbative contribution, these matrix elements are sums of Feynman integrals. In this way, the transversally-intersecting case fits naturally into the
S
-matrix bootstrap picture where singularities of higher-order diagrams are built up from lower-order ones.
This Landau diagram has been studied in integrable theories in Ref.
Coleman:1978kk
where the blobs were exact
S
-matrix elements.

Now let us show that all possible pairs of sequential discontinuities of Feynman integrals with generic masses come from one-vertex reducible Landau diagrams, by proving Lemma
3
. We begin by considering the commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\kappa}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\kappa^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G^{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\kappa}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\kappa^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}

(7.33)

that can be constructed for any pair of compatible contractions. The Landau loop equations associated with these contractions can be written as

\sum_{e\in E(\ker{\kappa^{\prime}})}\alpha_{e}b_{ce}q_{e}^{\mu}=0,\qquad\forall c\in\widehat{C}(\ker{\kappa^{\prime}})

(7.34)

and

\sum_{e\in E(\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})}\alpha_{e}b_{ce}q_{e}^{\mu}=0,\qquad\forall c\in\widehat{C}(\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})\,,

(7.35)

respectively. Notably, a loop momentum in
\widehat{C}(\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})
cannot have any edges in
E(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}})
, but a cycle which
contracts
to a cycle in
\widehat{C}(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}})
may have an edge in
E(\ker{\kappa^{\prime\prime}})
.
Thus, the circuit matrix for
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
must take the form

b_{ce}(\ker\kappa)=\begin{array}[]{ccc}&E(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})&E(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}})\\
\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})&\ast&0\\
\widehat{C}(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime}}}})&\ast&\ast\\
\end{array}\,,

(7.36)

where the blocks which do not necessarily vanish are marked by
\ast
.
Moreover, because the intersection is transversal and the monodromies commute, we can use the same argument with
{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
swapped conclude that the matrix
b_{ce}(\ker\kappa)
can also be written in the form

b_{ce}(\ker\kappa)=\begin{array}[]{ccc}&E(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}})&E(\ker{\kappa^{\prime}})\\
\widehat{C}(\ker{\overline{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}})&\ast&\ast\\
\widehat{C}(\ker{\kappa^{\prime}})&0&\ast\\
\end{array}\,.

(7.37)

Using the fact that
\ker\kappa^{\prime}=\ker\bar{\kappa}^{\prime}
and
\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime}=\ker\bar{\kappa}^{\prime\prime}
, we conclude that the circuit matrix for the kernel of the combined contraction
\kappa
must be block diagonal:

b_{ce}(\ker\kappa)=\begin{array}[]{ccc}&E(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})&E(\ker\kappa^{\prime})\\
\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})&\ast&0\\
\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa^{\prime})&0&\ast\\
\end{array}\,.

(7.38)

Thus,
\ker\kappa
can be written as a direct sum of
\ker\kappa^{\prime}
and
\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime}
, namely
b(\ker\kappa)=b(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})\oplus b(\ker\kappa^{\prime})
. This also gives us a
canonical
decomposition of the loop momenta
\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa)=\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime})\oplus\widehat{C}(\ker\kappa^{\prime})
, showing that for general kinematics, the two singularities
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime}}
and
\mathcal{P}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}
are incompatible if the fundamental circuits of their kernels are not disjoint. In other words, the Landau diagram corresponding to the contraction
\kappa
must factorize into two diagrams, and it is therefore one-vertex reducible. This proves Lemma
3
.

Note that the factorization property of Lemma
3
implies that the kernels of compatible contractions can be put in short exact sequences with the kernel of the combined contraction:

\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime}\rightarrowtail\ker\kappa\twoheadrightarrow\ker\kappa^{\prime}\,,\qquad\ker\kappa^{\prime}\rightarrowtail\ker\kappa\twoheadrightarrow\ker\kappa^{\prime\prime}\,.

(7.39)

For the bow-tie diagram in Fig.
18
the sequences are:

Contractions of a box singularity to the bubble
s
and

-channel singularities. In this case the kernels of the horizontal (or vertical) contractions are not the same as graphs; one is connected and the other is disconnected. However, for the special kinematics the kernels impose the same constraints.

The Steinmann relations famously state that amplitudes cannot have double discontinuities in partially-overlapping momentum channels
Steinmann
;
Steinmann2
;
Cahill:1973qp
. For instance, the double discontinuity of the box diagram with respect to the
s
and
t
channels must vanish in the physical region. These types of restrictions have been found to provide extremely powerful constraints for bootstrap approaches to computing amplitudes in recent years
Caron-Huot:2016owq
, and thus it is interesting to see how these relations also follow from Theorem
5
. At the same time, we will be able to see that Theorem
5
implies constraints on the sequential discontinuities of Feynman integrals that also go beyond the Steinmann relations.

We begin by drawing the Pham diagram for the
s
and
t
channel discontinuities of the box integral in Fig.
19
. We can see from this construction that
\ker\kappa^{t}\neq\ker\overline{\kappa^{t}}
and
\ker\kappa^{s}\neq\ker\overline{\kappa^{s}}
, which implies that
\kappa^{s}
and
\kappa^{t}
are incompatible.
Thus, setting all the internal masses in the box to be equal for simplicity (it is easy to check that the Pham loci remain separated in
(s,t)
space), we conclude that

This relation will hold for the box diagram in the physical region, or similarly for any other diagram that can be contracted to the box diagram. It is not hard to convince oneself that pairs of partially-overlapping momentum channels always give rise to incompatible contractions in the same way, implying that these pairs of sequential discontinuities must always vanish according to Theorem
5
.

To see an example in which Theorem
5
goes beyond the Steinmann relations, let us again consider the box diagram. In general, this diagram can be taken to describe a high-point scattering process with many different particles incoming or outgoing at each vertex, which implies that the kinematic variables
s
,

,

,
p_{2}^{2}
,
p_{3}^{2}

p_{4}^{2}
are all independent, where
p_{i}^{2}
is the momentum flowing in to vertex
i
. In Fig.

, we draw the Pham diagram that describes the computation of sequential discontinuities around
p_{1}^{2}=4m^{2}
and
p_{3}^{2}=4m^{2}
. If we take the process being described to be
4\to 4
, the quadruple cut through the box diagram can be realized in the physical region, which is to say with physical on-shell momenta, if two of the corner Mandelstam invariants, say
p_{2}^{2}
and
p_{4}^{2}
are negative. Since the kernels in this Pham diagram are not equal, we get a new restriction

(7.42)

The Pham relations therefore show that the monodromy around
p_{1}^{2}-4m^{2}=0
followed by the one around
p_{3}^{2}-4m^{2}=0
is zero, despite these channels not being overlapping.

It is instructive to compare these results with the formula for the Mandelstam double dispersion relation in Ref.
mandelstam1959analytic
, in which it is shown that the sequential discontinuity in
s
and
t
of the scalar box diagram
I_{\square}
is nonzero. This is not in any contradiction with the result presented here for two reasons. First, as discussed in Ref.
mandelstam1959analytic
, the support of the double-spectral density
\rho(s,t)\equiv\text{Disc}_{t}\text{Disc}_{s}I_{\square}
is outside of the physical region, so that analytic continuation of
\text{Disc}_{s}I_{\square}
is required to get to the non-vanishing region of
\rho(s,t)
. Second, the second discontinuity in
t
has support only above the threshold for the box singularity. So the sequential monodromy corresponding to
\rho(s,t)
is really the one taken first around the bubble singularity at
s=4m^{2}
, followed by the one around the box singularity at
4st\big[st-4m^{2}(s+t)+12m^{2}\big]=0
, where we have assumed that both internal and external masses are equal to
m
, for simplicity.
This sequential monodromy around the box threshold is in agreement with the predictions by Pham, and Eq. (
7.41
) is not violated, even outside of its proven validity in the physical region. A recent discussion about the validity and extension of the double spectral function can be found in Refs.
Correia:2020xtr
;
Correia:2021etg
.

7.6
Discussion

In this section (and in Sec.
6
), we have made a number of technical assumptions in order to be able to make rigorous statements about when sequential discontinuities vanish. However, one can certainly consider situations in which Pham loci are not principal, masses are not generic, singularities are not in the physical region, or singular loci overlap. Indeed, in most theories of physical or mathematical interest such as QCD or supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, the assumptions we have made for Theorems
2
,
7.7
, and
5
are violated. However, one can still extract some general lessons from these results, that will allow us to approach examples in which no general theorems yet exist.

In this respect, the main takeaway from this section is that when two contractions are compatible the associated singularities factorize, meaning that both sets of Landau equations can be simultaneously satisfied without increasing the codimension of the individual solutions. This property is key to understanding the nested singularity structure of Feynman integrals, or, more ambitiously, the
S
-matrix. Note that it is possible for the Landau equations to be compatible in this way even if the contractions associated with a pair of singularities are not compatible, when considering non-generic external kinematics. In such situations, sequential discontinuities can still be nonzero. We next turn to some more detailed considerations of such situations that go beyond the theorems discussed so far.

8
Generalizations

In this paper, we have mostly focused on singularities that occur in the physical region, and on studying integrals in generic kinematics. In this section, we peek beyond these restrictions. To do this, we leverage the intuition we have gained by thinking about Landau singularities as critical values in order to understand how sequential discontinuities can newly appear for restricted kinematics. For example, the projection along the
z
axis from a two-sphere has critical points at the North and South poles. But if we restrict the domain by cutting the sphere with a plane, we can see that it is easy to obtain new critical points. This information is contained implicitly in the Landau equations, but it is not geometrically obvious.

There are many motivations for studying special kinematics. These include:

•

Calculations often simplify in special kinematics, and the value of Feynman integrals and amplitudes in special kinematics can sometimes be used to bootstrap these quantities
Caron-Huot:2020bkp
.

•

Mathematical features that don’t arise in generic kinematics until higher loop orders, such as effective (transversal) intersections of singularity loci, can be simulated and studied in special kinematic configurations already at one loop.

•

One can explore regions which are not physical, such as
(2,2)
spacetime signature, which has been useful for understanding twistor constructions and in which massless three-point vertices can be naturally accommodated.

•

Feynman integrals that evaluate to special functions that go beyond multiple polylogarithms often simplify to polylogarithmic expressions in special kinematics. The techniques developed in this paper for studying Landau singularities may make it possible to systematically find kinematic limits in which these simplifications occur. For example, the two-loop sunrise integral, which is generically elliptic, reduces to multiple polylogarithms at the pseudo-threshold
Bloch:2013tra
.

We will not explore examples of all these possibilities here. Rather, we focus on exploring the key idea from Sec.
7.3
, that sequential discontinuities can only occur when the Landau equations that encode two singularities are compatible. In particular, we will consider two examples in which new double discontinuities appear in special kinematics where the Landau equations that encode these singularities become compatible, as shown in Fig.
21
, despite the fact that the incompatibility of the corresponding contractions restrict these discontinuities from appearing in generic kinematics.

\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime}}}
\mathcal{P}_{{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}}
p_{1}
p_{2}
k

Figure 21:
While the transversally-intersecting Pham loci

do not lead to compatible solutions of the Landau equations for generic masses (as illustrated in Fig.
